claim: The Drosophila genome encodes at least eight putative ZIP proteins.
source: BLASTP searches using the amino acid sequences of mammalian ZIP family members revealed that the Drosophila genome encodes at least eight putative ZIP proteins (Lye et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work (Lye et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2013).

claim: The protein encoded by CG7816 shares 45% identity and 58% similarity with human ZIP13.
source: Among them, the protein encoded by CG7816 shares the highest overall homology with human ZIP13 (45% identity and 58% similarity) (Figure 1A), and was named dZIP13 accordingly.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: dZIP13 belongs to the LIV-1 subfamily of zinc transporters.
source: In the phylogenetic tree, dZIP13 clusters together with hZIP13 and several other members including catsup (CG10449) and hZIP7 (Figure 1B), all belonging to the LIV-1 subfamily of zinc transporters or LZT proteins (Taylor and Nicholson, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B and citation to Taylor and Nicholson, 2003.

claim: dZIP13 has eight transmembrane domains.
source: Several typical features of ZIP family members (Jeong and Eide, 2013) are found in dZIP13, including eight transmembrane domains (TM), particularly amphipathic TM4 and TM5, and a predicted extracellular/luminal location of both the amino and carboxyl termini.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis and citation to Jeong and Eide, 2013.

claim: dZIP13 has only a single His residue in the histidine-rich region between TM3 and TM4.
source: Notably for dZIP13 and hZIP13, there is only a single His residue in a generally histidine-rich region (2–14 His) between TM3 and TM4.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis data.

claim: dZIP13 contains the conserved HEXXH metalloprotease motif within TM5.
source: The highly conserved potential metalloprotease His-Glu-X-X-His (HEXXH, where X is any amino acid) motif, located within TM5 (Bin et al., 2011) of LZT proteins, is also found in dZIP13 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1A and citation to Bin et al., 2011.

claim: Midgut-specific knockdown of dZIP13 reduces whole body iron levels to about 50% of normal.
source: Compared to the control, the iron levels in the dZIP13-RNAi fly dropped to about 50% of the normal iron content, while iron amount in overexpressing fly increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP-MS measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Midgut-specific modulation of dZIP13 expression does not alter zinc or copper levels in the whole body.
source: However, when dZIP13 was tissue specifically knocked down or over-expressed with NP3084-Gal4, a driver specifically expressing the activator Gal4 and thus modulating dZIP13 in the midgut region, the iron levels of the whole body changed dramatically while the amount of zinc level stayed unaltered (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by metal content measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ubiquitous RNAi of dZIP13 produces developmental arrest in the pupal stage with only about 10% eclosion rate.
source: Under normal dietary conditions, ubiquitous RNAi of dZIP13 by daughterless (Da-Gal4) produced developmental arrest in the pupal stage (only about 10% eclosion rate) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dietary iron supplementation rescues the eclosion defect of dZIP13-RNAi flies from ~10% to ~75%.
source: Amazingly, the eclosion defect resulting from dZIP13 knockdown could be rescued from ∼10% to ∼75% simply through dietary iron supplementation in the form of ferric ammonium citrate (FAC) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of iron chelator BPS exacerbates the eclosion defect of dZIP13-RNAi flies.
source: Addition of 0.1 mM iron-specific chelator bathophenanthrolinedisulfonic acid disodium (BPS), on the other hand, exacerbated the phenotype as an even lower eclosion rate was observed (Figure 2B), indicating abnormal iron absorption indeed plays a critical role in causing the eclosion defect in dZIP13-RNAi flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Zinc addition to the diet reduces the eclosion rate of dZIP13-RNAi flies to ~0%.
source: When zinc was added to the diet, almost no adult flies could eclose (∼0% eclosion rate); however, addition of zinc chelator TPEN could ameliorate the phenotype slightly, although without statistical significance (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Iron absorption can be competitively inhibited by additional zinc.
source: There have been several reports showing that iron absorption can be competitively inhibited by additional zinc (Rossander-Hulten et al., 1991; Whittaker, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Simultaneous addition of both zinc and iron rescues the eclosion defect of dZIP13-RNAi flies to ~65% eclosion rate.
source: Simultaneous addition of both zinc and iron could still rescue the eclosion defect very effectively (∼65% eclosion rate, statistically insignificant with iron only).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data.

claim: Wild type flies' eclosion rate remains unchanged with iron or zinc supplementation or deficiency.
source: The wild type flies' eclosion rate, in contrast, remained the same either in iron supplemented or deficient, zinc supplemented or deficient food (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Iron supplementation prolongs the median lifespan of dZIP13-RNAi flies from ~4 days to ~25 days.
source: Consistent with the results obtained in the eclosion experiments, the lifespan of dZIP13-RNAi flies was also prolonged by iron addition in the food (Figure 2D): the flies raised on iron supplemented food have a prolonged median lifespan (∼25 days) compared with files raised on normal food (∼4 days).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Zinc addition to the diet shortens the lifespan of dZIP13-RNAi flies to a median of ~1 day.
source: Addition of zinc to the diet shortened their lifespan (median lifespan of ∼1 day).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data.

claim: Cytosolic aconitase activity is an indicator of cytosolic iron levels.
source: Cytosolic aconitase needs to bind iron for its enzymatic activity and is an indicator of the cytosolic iron level (Haile et al., 1992; Tong and Rouault, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: dZIP13-RNAi larvae exhibit ~35% more cytosolic aconitase activity in the gut compared to control larvae.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, dZIP13-RNAi larvae exhibited ∼35% more c-aconitase activity in the gut as compared to the control larvae while dZIP13-OE larvae showed ∼20% c-aconitase activity reduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: dZIP13-OE larvae show ~20% reduction in cytosolic aconitase activity in the gut.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, dZIP13-RNAi larvae exhibited ∼35% more c-aconitase activity in the gut as compared to the control larvae while dZIP13-OE larvae showed ∼20% c-aconitase activity reduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cytosolic aconitase activity is significantly reduced in the whole body minus gut of dZIP13-RNAi larvae.
source: In contrast to this finding, in the remaining body parts (i.e., the whole body minus the gut) of dZIP13-RNAi larvae, c-aconitase activity was significantly reduced when compared to the control larvae, implying a general lack of iron in the body parts other than the gut.
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cytosolic aconitase activity is significantly elevated in the whole body minus gut of dZIP13-OE larvae.
source: Conversely, c-aconitase activity was significantly elevated in dZIP13-OE, implying an iron elevation in the other body parts (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Under iron deficiency, ferritin is down-regulated and Malvolio is up-regulated.
source: Under iron deficiency, ferritin and iron uptake protein Malvolio (Mvl) is respectively down- and up-regulated, while under iron surplus, vice versa (Figure 3C) (Missirlis et al., 2007; Tang and Zhou, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C and citations to published work.

claim: When dZIP13 is knocked down, ferritin is significantly up-regulated and Malvolio is down-regulated in the gut.
source: Indeed, when dZIP13 was knocked-down, ferritin was significantly up-regulated while Mvl down-regulated, very much akin to the scenario when the larvae were fed with iron-supplemented diet (Figure 3D, also see Figure 4E for ferritin protein levels).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both the gut and the rest of the body exhibit iron reduction after dZIP13 knockdown.
source: To directly quantify the total iron amount, we further performed ICP-MS (inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry) analysis of the gut and other body parts (whole body-gut). Both the gut and the rest of the body as a whole exhibited iron reduction after dZIP13 knockdown and iron increase when dZIP13 was overexpressed (Figure 3E and Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP-MS data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Both the gut and the rest of the body exhibit iron increase when dZIP13 is overexpressed.
source: To directly quantify the total iron amount, we further performed ICP-MS (inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry) analysis of the gut and other body parts (whole body-gut). Both the gut and the rest of the body as a whole exhibited iron reduction after dZIP13 knockdown and iron increase when dZIP13 was overexpressed (Figure 3E and Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP-MS data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Ferritin is the major iron storage protein in Drosophila and is located in the secretory pathway.
source: Because ferritin is the major iron storage protein and is located in the secretory pathway in Drosophila, we speculate that when dZIP13 is down-regulated in the gut, iron may not be able to move from the cytosol to the secretory compartments, resulting in iron elevation in the cytosol, a feedback control of iron uptake and an overall reduction of iron in both the gut and the rest of the body.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ferritin in Drosophila.

claim: Ferritin can accommodate thousands of iron atoms in its protein shell in the ferric form.
source: Ferritin, a heteropolymer composed of H and L subunits, can accommodate thousands of iron atoms in its protein shell in the ferric form.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ferritin structure and function.

claim: Ferritin is the major cytosolic iron-storage protein in mammalian organisms.
source: Ferritin is thought to be the major cytosolic iron-storage protein in mammalian organisms (Andrews, 2005; Knovich et al., 2009), while in Drosophila, unlike mammals, ferritin sequences of both the H and L chains contain secretion signals, confining them to the secretory pathway and making them abundant in the hemolymph (Nichol et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Drosophila ferritin sequences contain secretion signals that confine them to the secretory pathway.
source: Ferritin is thought to be the major cytosolic iron-storage protein in mammalian organisms (Andrews, 2005; Knovich et al., 2009), while in Drosophila, unlike mammals, ferritin sequences of both the H and L chains contain secretion signals, confining them to the secretory pathway and making them abundant in the hemolymph (Nichol et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nichol et al., 2002.

claim: A major function of Drosophila ferritin is absorption of dietary iron through iron loading and transporting via the secretory pathway.
source: A major function of Drosophila ferritin is absorption of dietary iron through iron loading and transporting via the secretory pathway supplying iron for the systemic use (Tang and Zhou, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang and Zhou, 2013b.

claim: In the iron cell region of dZIP13-RNAi larvae, no obvious iron signal could be detected.
source: In the iron cell region (a cluster of cells in the middle midgut region where iron absorption occurs) of dZIP13-RNAi larvae, we were unable to detect obvious iron signal, whereas a distinct blue iron-staining signal could be observed in the normal fly larvae (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement1), suggesting a lack of iron incorporation into ferritin after dZIP13 interference.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferric iron staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpression of dZIP13 leads to stronger iron staining in the iron cell region and ectopically in the anterior midgut.
source: Conversely, overexpression of dZIP13 led to a stronger staining in the iron cell region, and ectopically in the anterior midgut (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferric iron staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: High iron levels (5 mM FAC) can induce ectopic ferric iron staining in the anterior midgut.
source: This result is reminiscent of the observation that high iron levels, such as 5 mM FAC, can also induce ectopic ferric iron staining in the anterior midgut, suggesting an iron accumulation occurs in the secretory pathway of the gut cells when dZIP13 is overexpressed.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the study.

claim: Under high levels of dietary iron, iron is only faintly stained in dZIP13-RNAi larvae.
source: Under high levels of dietary iron, iron was only faintly stained in the dZIP13-RNAi larvae, whereas staining was much stronger in dZIP13 overexpression larvae (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ferric iron staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Intestinal ferritin is poorly loaded with iron in dZIP13-RNAi larvae.
source: A native-PAGE staining for ferric iron further confirmed that the intestinal ferritin was indeed poorly loaded with iron in the dZIP13-RNAi larvae while the iron loading in the dZIP13-OE larvae was mildly elevated (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement2).
evidence: The claim is supported by native-PAGE ferric iron staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Iron loading in ferritin is mildly elevated in dZIP13-OE larvae.
source: A native-PAGE staining for ferric iron further confirmed that the intestinal ferritin was indeed poorly loaded with iron in the dZIP13-RNAi larvae while the iron loading in the dZIP13-OE larvae was mildly elevated (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement2).
evidence: The claim is supported by native-PAGE ferric iron staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In flies reared with standard food, GFP-tagged ferritin is most prominently expressed in the iron cell region.
source: As shown in Figure 4D and reported previously (Missirlis et al., 2007), in flies reared with standard food, GFP-tagged ferritin was most prominently expressed in the iron cell region.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and citation to Missirlis et al., 2007.

claim: When dZIP13 expression is knocked down, ferritin is ectopically and significantly induced in the anterior and posterior midguts.
source: When dZIP13 expression was knocked down, expression of ferritin was ectopically and significantly induced in the anterior and posterior midguts, and was constitutively expressed in the iron cell region (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A dramatic increase of ferritin level is seen in dZIP13-RNAi larvae by Western blot.
source: Induction of ferritin expression in dZIP13-RNAi larvae was confirmed with a Western blot using a ferritin antibody against ferritin. A dramatic increase of ferritin level was seen in dZIP13-RNAi larvae, with a decrease observed in the dZIP13-OE larvae (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A decrease in ferritin level is observed in dZIP13-OE larvae by Western blot.
source: Induction of ferritin expression in dZIP13-RNAi larvae was confirmed with a Western blot using a ferritin antibody against ferritin. A dramatic increase of ferritin level was seen in dZIP13-RNAi larvae, with a decrease observed in the dZIP13-OE larvae (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement4).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Midgut-specific ferritin RNAi causes decreased total body iron contents, retarded growth, and death of most progeny at the larval or pupal stage.
source: Ferritin RNAi with gut-specific driver (NP3084) causes decreased total body iron contents, retarded growth, and death of most of the progeny at the larval or pupal stage (Tang and Zhou, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang and Zhou, 2013b.

claim: The eclosion rate of midgut-specific ferritin RNAi flies can be rescued from <5% to ~30% through overexpressing dZIP13.
source: Notably, the eclosion rate of these flies could be rescued from <5–30% through overexpressing dZIP13 (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The decreased total body iron content of midgut-specific ferritin RNAi larvae can be partially rescued by dZIP13 overexpression.
source: Consistently, the decreased total body iron content of midgut-specific ferritin RNAi larvae could also be partially rescued by dZIP13 overexpression (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by metal content data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: hZIP13 has been reported to be located in Golgi and some intracellular vesicles.
source: Locations of hZIP13 have been reported in Golgi and some intracellular vesicles (Fukada et al., 2008; Jeong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: C-terminal myc-tagged dZIP13 partially overlaps with ER and Golgi in Caco2 cells.
source: To examine the intracellular position of dZIP13, a C-terminal myc-tagged dZIP13 was introduced into human intestinal Caco2 cells. Immunofluorescence staining indicated it partially overlapped with ER and Golgi (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: C-terminal tagged dZIP13-EGFP is functional and partially located to the Golgi apparatus in flies.
source: A similarly tagged (at the C-terminal) dZIP13-EGFP was made and expressed in the flies and shown to be functional. This dZIP13-EGFP is also partially located to the Golgi apparatus (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Endogenous dZIP13 shows obvious overlapping with ER/Golgi apparatus in the Drosophila gut.
source: To check the intracellular positions of endogenous dZIP13 in the Drosophila gut, we generated an antibody against dZIP13. The specificity of the antibody was confirmed by significantly reduced staining in dZIP13-RNAi larvae and loss of staining in dZIP13 mutant. Once more we observed an obvious overlapping of dZIP13 with the ER/Golgi apparatus in the Drosophila gut staining, along with some staining in additional intracellularlocations (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Co-localization of dZIP13 with endosome markers is poor.
source: Co-localization of dZIP13 with endosome markers, however, was poor (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The iron level of ER/Golgi is reduced in dZIP13-RNAi larvae and increased in dZIP13-OE larvae.
source: Metal content of ER/Golgi was tested and results showed that the iron level of these compartments was indeed reduced in dZIP13-RNAi and increased in dZIP13-OE larvae (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by metal content measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Zinc level in ER/Golgi is marginally altered and negatively correlated to iron levels when dZIP13 expression is modulated.
source: Zinc level was marginally altered in these compartments, but negatively correlated to iron levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by metal content measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of dZIP13 in E. coli results in very poor growth under normal conditions.
source: Interestingly, expression of dZIP13 in E. coli resulted in very poor growth under normal conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth data.

claim: Growth of E. coli expressing dZIP13 is partially restored in iron replete conditions.
source: Strikingly, growth was partially restored in iron replete conditions whereas zinc had no effect (Figure 6A), indicating the lack of growth of E. coli with dZIP13 expression was due to intracellular iron deficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: dZIP13 expression renders E. coli more resistant to iron stresses.
source: dZIP13 expression also rendered E. coli more resistant to iron stresses compared with the control (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Expression of dZIP13 in E. coli reduces cellular iron levels in iron-rich medium.
source: Further analysis of cellular iron contents indicated that with iron-rich medium (2 mM iron), expression of dZIP13 reduced the iron level of the cells, while the change of zinc was insignificant (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by metal content measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ferroportin has been successfully shown to mediate iron export in Xenopus oocytes using Fe isotopes.
source: Ferroportin, a plasma membrane iron exporter, for example, has been successfully shown to mediate iron export in Xenopus oocytes, by using Fe isotopes and measuring intracellular and extracellular radioactivity levels (Donovan et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Donovan et al., 2000.

claim: The amount of iron exported from E. coli expressing dZIP13 increases roughly linearly within the tested time and is significantly higher than control.
source: A time-course study of iron transportation in E. coli expressing dZIP13 is shown in Figure 7A. The amount of iron exported from E. coli expressing dZIP13 increased roughly linearly within the tested time and was significantly higher in comparison to the control.
evidence: The claim is supported by radioisotope transport assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: dZIP13 is located on the membrane of E. coli cells when expressed.
source: Labeling with anti-dZIP13 indicates that dZIP13 was indeed located on the membrane of E. coli cells, while control with the empty vector was with minimal signal (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The rate of iron uptake into ER/Golgi is much higher in dZIP13-OE samples and lower in dZIP13-RNAi samples.
source: The results shown in Figure 7D indicate that the iron uptake of ER/Golgi isolated from dZIP13-OE Drosophila larvae was significantly increased whereas that from dZIP13-RNAi was decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by radioisotope transport assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: A linear correlation between time and radioactivity is observed in ER/Golgi iron uptake assays.
source: Again, a linear correlation between time and radioactivity was observed.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the radioisotope transport assay.

claim: dZIP13 shares the highest homology with human ZIP13.
source: Bioinformatics analysis indicates that dZIP13 shares the highest homology with human ZIP13 (Figure 1A, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: hZIP13 overexpression in Drosophila leads to a decrease of overall aconitase activity.
source: Indeed, hZIP13 overexpression in Drosophila also led to a decrease of overall aconitase activity (Figure 8A), suggesting hZIP13 similarly affected iron metabolism in Drosophila.
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity assay data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Expression of hZIP13 rescues the eclosion rate of dZIP13-RNAi larvae from 40% to 75%.
source: Moreover, a survival assay showed that expression of hZIP13 rescued the eclosion rate of dZIP13-RNAi larvae from 40% to 75% (Figure 8B), and doubled the lifespan of dZIP13-RNAi flies (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by eclosion rate data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression of hZIP13 doubles the lifespan of dZIP13-RNAi flies.
source: Moreover, a survival assay showed that expression of hZIP13 rescued the eclosion rate of dZIP13-RNAi larvae from 40% to 75% (Figure 8B), and doubled the lifespan of dZIP13-RNAi flies (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: hZIP7 is closely related to ZIP13.
source: Another member of the ZIP family, hZIP7, is closely related to ZIP13 (Figure 1B) and has been shown to be a zinc importer located on the ER/Golgi (Taylor et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B and citations to published work.

claim: hZIP7 has been shown to be a zinc importer located on the ER/Golgi.
source: Another member of the ZIP family, hZIP7, is closely related to ZIP13 (Figure 1B) and has been shown to be a zinc importer located on the ER/Golgi (Taylor et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2004 and Huang et al., 2005.

claim: Expression of hZIP7 produces neither whole body aconitase activity change nor rescues the defects of dZIP13-RNAi flies.
source: However, despite similarity to hZIP13, expression of hZIP7 produced neither whole body aconitase activity change, nor rescued the defects of dZIP13-RNAi flies (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity and eclosion/lifespan data shown in Figures 8A-C.

claim: hZIP13 mutations cause SCD-EDS, a disease with defective collagen hydroxylation.
source: hZIP13 mutations cause SCD-EDS, a disease with defective collagen hydroxylation leading to a decrease of collagen cross-linking and secretion.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about SCD-EDS.

claim: Type IV collagen is the main constituent of basement membrane in Drosophila.
source: Type IV collagen, the main constituent of basement membrane, is encoded by two collagen genes Viking (Vkg) and Cg25C, which are expressed in Drosophila fat bodies.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila collagen.

claim: dPlod is expressed in collagen-producing cells and participates in the assembly and secretion of collagen.
source: dPlod is expressed in the collagen-producing cells (Bunt et al., 2011), and participates in the assembly and secretion of collagen.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bunt et al., 2011.

claim: Ubiquitous knockdown of dZIP13 causes substantial retention of Vkg-GFP in fat body cells.
source: Ubiquitous knockdown of dZIP13 caused substantial retention of Vkg-GFP in the fat body cells, while iron supplementation rescued the Vkg-GFP retention (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Iron supplementation rescues the Vkg-GFP retention caused by dZIP13 knockdown.
source: Ubiquitous knockdown of dZIP13 caused substantial retention of Vkg-GFP in the fat body cells, while iron supplementation rescued the Vkg-GFP retention (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Iron is an important cofactor/co-substrate of lysyl hydroxylase.
source: Because iron is an important cofactor/co-substrate of lysyl hydroxylase, a critical enzyme in collagen synthesis (Figure 8E) (Murad et al., 1985), the observation of iron reduction in ER/Golgi when dZIP13 is inhibited (Figure 5D) suggests that the normal functions of lysyl hydroxylase and prolyl hydroxylase might be compromised under iron shortage (see 'Discussion' for more).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Murad et al., 1985 and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: dZIP13 is the Drosophila orthologue of hZIP13.
source: Taken together, our results indicate dZIP13 is analogous to hZIP13, and is truly the Drosophila orthologue of hZIP13.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results showing functional similarity.

claim: The functions of dZIP13 and hZIP13 are fundamentally different from those of other zinc importers including ZIP7.
source: Their functions are fundamentally different from those of the other zinc importers including the closely related ZIP7.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results showing different functional outcomes.

claim: dZIP13 mediates iron export to the secretory pathway.
source: We presented substantial evidence establishing that dZIP13 mediates iron export to the secretory pathway, identifying dZIP13 as the elusive iron transporter in the secretory pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: This is the first time a member of the ZIP transporter family has been reported to function as an iron exporter.
source: Moreover, this is the first time to report that a member of the ZIP transporter family functions as an iron exporter.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: ZIP14 and ZIP8 have been reported to be capable of transporting iron.
source: Previously, certain members of ZIPs, such as ZIP14 (Liuzzi et al., 2006) and ZIP8 (Wang et al., 2012), have been reported to be capable of transporting iron.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: ZIP14 and ZIP8 are complex, broad-scope metal-ion importers and their in vivo involvement in iron homeostasis is yet to be established.
source: However, they are only complex, broad-scope metal-ion importers and their in vivo involvement in iron homeostasis is yet to be established.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of existing literature on ZIP14 and ZIP8.

claim: Dietary iron uptake in Drosophila gut is mediated by secreted ferritin and requires iron loading in the secretory pathway.
source: The unanticipated finding of dZIP13 as an iron exporter was facilitated by the characteristic manner of dietary iron uptake in Drosophila gut, which is mediated by secreted ferritin and requires iron loading in the secretory pathway (Tang and Zhou, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang and Zhou, 2013b.

claim: In mammals, ferritin is predominantly localized in the cytosol for storing cytosolic iron.
source: In mammals, ferritin is predominantly localized in the cytosol for storing cytosolic iron, and absorbed dietary iron is effluxed from enterocytes through ferroportin (Vanoaica et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Vanoaica et al., 2010.

claim: In insects, ferritin is mainly secreted and plays a central role in iron absorption.
source: However, in insects such as Drosophila, ferritin is mainly secreted, playing a central role in iron absorption by bringing iron out of enterocytes and into the hemolymph through the secretory pathway (Tang and Zhou, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang and Zhou, 2013b.

claim: Zinc efflux protein ZnT5 can mediate zinc transport in both directions.
source: Considering the unusual nature of dZIP13 as an iron exporter while other members of the family (SLC39A) so far identified all appear to be importers, it is noteworthy that zinc efflux protein ZnT5 (SLC30A5) can mediate zinc transport in both directions (Valentine et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Valentine et al., 2007.

claim: The TM4 amino acid sequence for all ZIP13s is DNFTHG whereas other closely related ZIPs have HNFTDG.
source: The most notabe difference is in transmembrane domain TM4. The TM4 amino acid sequence for all ZIP13s are DNFTHG (Figure 9) whereas other closely related ZIPs are HNFTDG, i.e., the highly conserved region in TM4 has a D and H residue swap between ZIP13s and other ZIP members.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 9.

claim: When the D and H residues in TM4 are switched, dZIP13 is no longer functional.
source: Our preliminary evidences suggest this variation might be an important factor because when we switched this D and H dZIP13 was no longer functional.
evidence: The claim is based on preliminary experimental observations.

claim: Mutations in LH family genes have been found in Bruck syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos type VI.
source: Mutations in LH family genes have been found in several human diseases including Bruck syndrome (van der Slot et al., 2003; Ha-Vinh et al., 2004) (OMIM #609220) and Ehlers–Danlos type VI (Yeowell and Walker, 2000) (OMIM #225400).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Mutations in ZIP13 have been identified as the cause for SCD-EDS.
source: Recently mutations in ZIP13, a member of the SLC39A/Zrt-Irt-like protein (ZIP) family, have been identified as the cause for the spondylocheiro dysplastic Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (SCD-EDS), a form of EDS sharing some similar clinical presentations with EDS VI, which is caused by mutations in PLOD1 gene encoding lysyl hydroxylase (LH1) (Fukada et al., 2008; Giunta et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fukada et al., 2008 and Giunta et al., 2008.

claim: ZIP transporters were generally believed to import zinc into the cytosol from the extracellular milieu or organellar lumen.
source: Because ZIP transporters were generally believed to import zinc into the cytosol from the extracellular milieu or organellar lumen (Kambe et al., 2006; Lichten and Cousins, 2009; Jeong and Eide, 2013), the pathogenesis of SCD-EDS was difficult to understand and various hypotheses were proposed to explain how the zinc importer could affect iron homeostasis (Fukada et al., 2008; Giunta et al., 2008; Jeong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: SCD-EDS is likely due to impaired iron transport to ER/Golgi from ZIP13 mutations.
source: The identification of dZIP13 as the iron exporter for the secretory compartments suggests a more direct interpretation of SCD-EDS: ZIP13 mutations impair iron transport to ER/Golgi, significantly attenuating the activities of iron-requiring enzymes such as lysyl hydroxylase, leading to defective collagen synthesis and accumulation in the secretory pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about dZIP13 function.

claim: Lysyl and prolyl hydroxylase activities from cellular extracts of SCD-EDS patient cells were reported to be normal.
source: However, lysyl and prolyl hydroxylase activities from the cellular extracts of patient cells were reported to be normal (Giunta et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Giunta et al., 2008.

claim: Externally supplied iron is needed to perform lysyl and prolyl hydroxylase enzymatic assays.
source: It has been shown that externally supplied iron is needed to do these assays (Tuderman et al., 1977), suggesting iron is probably not tightly bound to these enzymes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tuderman et al., 1977.

claim: Addition of iron in enzymatic assays would neutralize the original iron-deficient state of enzymes in vivo.
source: However, the addition of iron would neutralize or mask the original iron-deficienct state of these enzymes in vivo (in the ER/Golgi of SCD-EDS patient cells), and therefore produce 'normal' in vitro enzymatic activities despite defective in vivo hydroxylation.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the experimental conditions.

claim: Jeong et al. measured metal uptake activity of ZIP13 using mammalian cells.
source: Jeong et al. (2012) used mammalian cells to measure metal uptake activity of ZIP13.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jeong et al., 2012.

claim: In Jeong et al.'s experiment, zinc uptake was observed but iron failed to compete with zinc in the importing assay.
source: In that experiment, zinc uptake was observed, but iron failed to compete with zinc in the importing assay.
evidence: The claim is based on description of results from Jeong et al., 2012.

claim: Giunta et al., Fukada et al., and Bin et al. proposed zinc accumulation in ER/Golgi underlies SCD-EDS.
source: While Jeong et al. proposed zinc deficiency in the ER/Golgi, Giunta et al. (2008), Fukada et al. (2008), and Bin et al. (2011) proposed zinc accumulation in the ER/Golgi underlies SCD-EDS.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Zinc has been reported as an inhibitor of prolyl hydroxylase.
source: Indeed, zinc has been reported as an inhibitor of prolyl hydroxylase (Tuderman et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tuderman et al., 1977.

claim: Only a marginal increase of zinc in ER/Golgi was observed when dZIP13 was knocked down.
source: However in our hands, we saw only a marginal increase of zinc in the ER/Golgi when dZIP13 was knocked-down, but a much more dramatic change in the iron level.
evidence: The claim is supported by metal content measurements.

claim: Iron dyshomeostasis is probably the primary cause contributing to SCD-EDS.
source: We suggest iron dyshomeostasis instead of a zinc defect is probably the primary cause contributing to SCD-EDS.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: None of the classical iron phenotypes are observed in SCD-EDS patients.
source: Another issue worth pointing out is that none of the classical iron phenotypes are observed in SCD-EDS patients.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of SCD-EDS clinical presentation.

claim: Iron deficiency in SCD-EDS is possibly localized to the secretory pathway while cytosolic and mitochondrial iron levels remain not much affected.
source: In SCD-EDS, it is possible that iron deficiency is localized to the secretory pathway and cytosolic and mitochondrial iron levels remain not much affected.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the study's findings.

claim: A ZIP13 mutation would result in iron dyshomeostasis that would not present with typical iron deficiency symptoms.
source: Therefore, a ZIP13 mutation would result in a type of iron dyshomeostasis that would not present itself with the typical types of symptons (e.g., skin abnormality, bone malformation, and growth retardation) observed with classical iron deficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about ZIP13 function.

claim: Iron dyshomeostasis is likely involved in a wider spectrum of biological abnormalities than previously thought.
source: Nevertheless, our results add another level of complexity in the regulation of iron homeostasis and some of the consequences that arise from its disruption.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: Lysyl hydroxylase and collagen prolyl 4-hydroxylases are post-translational modifying enzymes localized to the lumen of endoplasmic reticulum.
source: For example, lysyl hydroxylase (LH, also referred to as PLOD) and collagen prolyl 4-hydroxylases (P4Hs) are two post-translational modifying enzymes localized to the lumen of endoplasmic reticulum, which use Fe2+ as a cofactor (Tuderman et al., 1977; Pirskanen et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Lysyl hydroxylase and prolyl 4-hydroxylases use Fe2+ as a cofactor.
source: For example, lysyl hydroxylase (LH, also referred to as PLOD) and collagen prolyl 4-hydroxylases (P4Hs) are two post-translational modifying enzymes localized to the lumen of endoplasmic reticulum, which use Fe2+ as a cofactor (Tuderman et al., 1977; Pirskanen et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Lysyl hydroxylase and prolyl hydroxylases are critical for the synthesis of collagen.
source: These two enzymes are critical for the synthesis of collagen, a crucial part of the basement membrane, and are formed by a complicated process involving multiple co- or post-translational modifications (Myllyharju and Kivirikko, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Myllyharju and Kivirikko, 2004.

claim: Only one type of collagen IV, encoded by Viking and Cg25C, is found in Drosophila.
source: While the types of collagens and genes found in mammals are very complex, only one type of collagen IV, encoded by two genes Viking (Vkg) and Cg25C, is found in Drosophila, and it constitutes a major structural component of basement membranes in the developing fly (Fessler and Fessler, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fessler and Fessler, 1989.

claim: Drosophila ferritin binds iron in the early secretory compartments and is then secreted into the circulation system.
source: In adidition to lysyl hydroxylase and prolyl hydroxylase, ferritin is another iron-dependent protein residing in the secretory pathway of Drosophila. In constrast to mammalian ferritin, which is predominantly found in the cytosol, Drosophila ferritin binds iron in the early secretory compartments and is then secreted into the circulation system (Mandilaras et al., 2013; Tang and Zhou, 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Ferritin secretion in Drosophila is central for systemic iron supply and tissue iron detoxification.
source: This process is central for systemic iron supply as well as tissue iron detoxification (Tang and Zhou, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tang and Zhou, 2013b.

claim: Drosophila carries a larger amount of iron through the secretory pathway compared to mammals.
source: Therefore, in comparison to mammals, it is expected that Drosophila will carry a larger amount of iron through this pathway and abnormalities in this process will lead to serious iron deficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differences in ferritin localization between Drosophila and mammals.

claim: The intracellular iron transfer process is not well understood.
source: The intracellular iron transfer process is not well understood, and the identity of the iron transporter responsible for iron delivery to the secretory compartments remains elusive.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The identity of the iron transporter responsible for iron delivery to the secretory compartments was elusive prior to this study.
source: The intracellular iron transfer process is not well understood, and the identity of the iron transporter responsible for iron delivery to the secretory compartments remains elusive.
evidence: The claim is based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Drosophila ZIP13 fulfills the iron effluxing role to the secretory compartments.
source: In this study, we show Drosophila ZIP13 (Slc39a13), a presumed zinc importer, fulfills the iron effluxing role.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes iron-rescuable iron absorption defect.
source: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes iron-rescuable iron absorption defect, simultaneous iron increase in the cytosol and decrease in the secretory compartments, failure of ferritin iron loading, and abnormal collagen secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes simultaneous iron increase in the cytosol and decrease in the secretory compartments.
source: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes iron-rescuable iron absorption defect, simultaneous iron increase in the cytosol and decrease in the secretory compartments, failure of ferritin iron loading, and abnormal collagen secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by aconitase activity assays and metal content measurements.

claim: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes failure of ferritin iron loading.
source: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes iron-rescuable iron absorption defect, simultaneous iron increase in the cytosol and decrease in the secretory compartments, failure of ferritin iron loading, and abnormal collagen secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by ferric iron staining and native-PAGE experiments.

claim: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes abnormal collagen secretion.
source: Interfering with dZIP13 expression causes iron-rescuable iron absorption defect, simultaneous iron increase in the cytosol and decrease in the secretory compartments, failure of ferritin iron loading, and abnormal collagen secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by Vkg-GFP retention experiments.

claim: dZIP13 expression in E. coli confers upon the host iron-dependent growth.
source: dZIP13 expression in E. coli confers upon the host iron-dependent growth and iron resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth experiments.

claim: dZIP13 expression in E. coli confers upon the host iron resistance.
source: dZIP13 expression in E. coli confers upon the host iron-dependent growth and iron resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial growth experiments.

claim: Time-coursed transport assays using an iron isotope indicated a potent iron exporting activity of dZIP13.
source: Importantly, time-coursed transport assays using an iron isotope indicated a potent iron exporting activity of dZIP13.
evidence: The claim is supported by radioisotope transport assay data.

claim: SCD-EDS is likely due to a failure of iron delivery to the secretory compartments.
source: The identification of dZIP13 as an iron transporter suggests that the spondylocheiro dysplastic form of Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, in which hZIP13 is defective, is likely due to a failure of iron delivery to the secretory compartments.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study's findings about dZIP13 function.
